pistons.headline: Pistons vs Magic final score: Detroit’s dominant defense shows up with Cade Cunningham sidelined
pistons.body:
ORLANDO, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 24: Isaiah Joe #17 of the Detroit Pistons reacts after scoring a three-pointer against the Orlando Magic during the fourth quarter of a Emirates NBA Cup game at Kia Center on November 24, 2026 in Orlando, Florida. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Rich Storry/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Goin to Work Pistons showed up tonight. Detroit dispatched the Orlando Magic 104-86. This was another statement game. It doesn’t matter who plays; defense travels. Detroit is now 2-1 in NBA Cup play with a plus-31 point differential. Orlando felt Detroit’s defensive wrath, holding Orlando to 14 second-quarter points. They were everywhere.

Cade Cunningham was a late scratch, but the next man steps up here. Both teams struggled to put the ball in the hoop, but Detroit generated better shots. They swung the ball from side to side on plenty of possessions. The shot-making results weren’t always there, but their process was solid. It was probably more than solid considering they were down three starters tonight.

Ausar Thompson and Daniss Jenkins picked up more on-ball reps. Jenkins had a 15-point and 10-assist double-double. Thompson continues to grow as a playmaker for others as he added seven more assists tonight.

Ausar seems much more sure of himself this season. Even the moments he turns down shots to find a teammate are telling — everything seems planned.

Ausar wasn’t the only Piston with an all-around A performance. Kevin Huerter finished with 13-5-6. He worked the off-ball screen here, slightly froze the big, and threw an accurate lob to Paul Reed.

The OOP 🎯 pic.twitter.com/VetSoIuf8f
— Detroit Pistons (@DetroitPistons) November 25, 2026

Isaiah Joe led the team with 21 points. He went 5-for-11 from trey. Joe showed off the range and confidence. He pressured the ball on the other end. Shooters competing on defense, and not being must-hide defenders, is such a plus. Joe is picking it up.

Ron Holland has success from deep. He buried two 3s. Detroit shot it well as a team despite their low point total. They went 15-for-36 from deep compared to Orlando’s 12-for-36. John Collins, Woo, and Elijah Harkless (he made some momentum-swinging ones) all hit two 3s.

Detroit knocked down 3s but kept Orlando from doing anything. Franz Wagner had been on a hot streak until he ran into this defense (29 PPG over the last 10). He (20 pts) and Desmond Bane (21 pts) put numbers on the board, but it wasn’t easy. Those two saw a crowd every time they drove the ball. Wagner started spamming push shots that felt automatic, but Detroit held him in check.

Anthony Black was a non-factor offensively tonight. That’s a testament to Detroit’s D, as he’s been rolling all year. The Magic missed so many shots at the rim. They were initially dominating Detroit on the offensive glass, but those missed shots eventually turned into Detroit run-outs.

The Pistons also got their hands on so many Magic passes tonight. They made Orlando creators play with multiple hands in their faces and trusted their closeouts to disrupt “open” Orlando 3s. Holding a team under 90 in 2026 is some Goin to Work stuff. Hats off to J.B. Bickerstaff for having this defense ready to go at all times.

Detroit’s final group play cup game is Friday versus the flaming hot Tyler Herro and the Milwaukee Bucks. Detroit could still win the group even after losing to the Toronto Raptors last Friday. They might need some help, but must start by handling their business with the Bucks.

Jalen Duren remains out as he works his way back from a hamstring strain. That’s unfortunate because I am desperate to see what this team looks like with Duren back in the fold and eager to leave behind the John Collins starting-center era for good. In Detroit’s most recent loss against the Atlanta Hawks, they were outrebounded by 19 and outscored in the paint 27-6. Tonight, they face the Orlando Magic. Orlando has righted the ship a bit, winning five of its past seven games. They win by protecting the paint, and that has been Detroit’s Achilles’ heel since Duren went down. They don’t let you score inside, and their defense is top 5 in limiting second-chance points, paint points, and fast-break points. Detroit is not going to find a clear path to easy points, which means their half-court offensive execution must improve significantly over their recent outings.

pistons.headline: Pistons at Hawks final score: Detroit outscored by 21 in the fourth, lose 107-97
pistons.body:
ATLANTA, GEORGIA - NOVEMBER 22: Nickeil Alexander-Walker #7 of the Atlanta Hawks reacts after hitting a three-point basket against the Detroit Pistons during the first quarter at State Farm Arena on November 22, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images

That was an unbelievable collapse by Detroit, and quite possibly the worst game of Cade Cunningham’s career.

The Pistons went into the fourth quarter with an 85-74 lead. They outscored the Hawks by 10 in the third quarter, and ESPN had Detroit at a 90% chance to win the game when the final frame started.

That went downhill quickly as the Hawks went on an 18-0 run to open the fourth quarter. The Pistons didn’t score their first points until Isaiah Joe hit a corner three with 4:52 left in the game. Detroit’s offense stalled, the ball wasn’t moving, and for whatever reason, Cade Cunningham and Daniss Jenkins took it upon themselves to try to iso Dyson Daniels and Lu Dort. As you can tell, it didn’t work.

Detroit shot better from the field, the three-point line, and the free-throw line. They even scored more points in the paint than the Hawks, but couldn’t manage to grab a rebound. Atlanta grabbed 19 more rebounds than Detroit and outrebounded the Pistons on the offensive glass 24-8. If there was ever a game that showed Detroit needed Jalen Duren back ASAP, this was it.

Atlanta had 10 more fastbreak points than Detroit, and second-chance points went in a massive favor of the Hawks to the tune of 27-6. Detroit’s rebounding was horrendous – outside of Ausar Thompson’s 11 boards, John Collins was second on the team with six.

Cade Cunningham scored in single digits for the first time all season with five points while shooting 2-for-9 from the field. He also added four rebounds and 15 assists in what is surely one of the weirdest stat lines of his career. Kevin Huerter was a -28 on the floor while shooting 1-for-8 for a measly two points.

Oddly enough, it was Isaiah Joe who led the team in scoring with 19 points on 15 attempts. Joe was +11 tonight and knocked down three threes. John Collins and Ausar Thompson each had 18 points. Collins made four threes, and Ausar added five assists. Paul Reed had 16 points off the bench, and Daniss Jenkins had 11.

In what should’ve been a victory tonight in Atlanta, Detroit blew their double-digit lead and deserved to lose this game. That was one of the worst fourth quarter performances I’ve ever watched, and it looked like a middle school team that couldn’t grab a rebound in a scrimmage against the high school varsity.

Please, Jalen Duren, come back soon.

Detroit moves to 10-6 on the year and will now travel to Orlando to take on the Magic on Tuesday night. Let’s hope this Pistons team has a short memory and burns tonight’s fourth quarter tape.

Go Stones.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Raptors final score: Cade vs. Scottie battle goes to Raps
pistons.body:
[DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 20: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons plays defense on Scottie Barnes #4 of the Toronto Raptors during the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup on November 20, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Chris Schwegler/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Two former teammates and two Eastern Conference teams traded body blows all night. A Cade Cunningham 3-pointer to put the Pistons up 102-101 with 20 seconds left was answered by a Scottie Barnes driving layup over two defenders to give the Raptors the lead they would not relinquish. When a Kevin Huerter three came up short as the buzzer sounded, it was decided. Raptors 105-102.

Cunningham led Detroit with 23 points and nine assists, but he was outshined on this night by his former Montverde teammate Barnes, who led all scorers with 29 points and hit his first nine shots of the night.

While it was appointment television watching the two top players on each team matched up with each other, the rest of the game was pretty much a horror show for the Pistons. Distilling why the Pistons dropped this game will sound very familiar to Pistons fans — not owning the paint.

Detroit surrendered 54 points inside to Toronto and gave up crucial offensive rebounds late. It’s one thing to see Barnes put a great game on you, but Detroit was owned inside by rookie Allen Graves making his first start of the season. He scored 20 points, had 10 rebounds, including four on the offensive end. Detroit simply had no answer for him. Certainly not John Collins.

The overmatched emergency starting center struggled again in just under 20 minutes of action. He was just 1-of-4 from the floor for three points and six rebounds. The return of Isaiah Joe from injury isn’t looking very different from when he was playing early in the season — he’s still struggling to find his shot. Joe was 1-of-6 from deep tonight. Getting those kinds of performances from your two highest-profile offseason acquisitions is not the recipe for winning basketball.

The other major issue tonight is that you were facing one of the worst-shooting offenses in the NBA and on this night, they could not miss. Some of that had to do with Detroit’s occasionally passive defense. But tonight, the Raptors players were just collectively on one. We already covered how hot Barnes was, especially early, but the sweet shooting was up and down the roster.

The rookie Graves was 6-of-9, Jakob Poeltl was 5-of-7, and Immanuel Quickly was 6-of-10. Collectively, Toronto shot 67% inside the arc tonight. Again, I’m going to point to the big black hole in the middle of Detroit’s lineup. A combination of John Collins and Paul Reed as your only big men is just not going to get it done in the NBA. The Pistons need Jalen Duren to come back desperately.

The loss to the Raptors drops the Pistons to 1-1 in NBA Cup play, but then again, I refuse to care about the NBA Cup. Detroit now goes on a mini road trip to Atlanta on Sunday and Orlando on Tuesday before enjoying seven of the next eight games at home.

The Toronto Raptors are scuffling in the first leg of the NBA season, but there is certainly a lot of talent there. Yes, Kawhi Leonard is absent with news of managing knee pain and swelling that surely puts a shiver up the spine of every Toronto fan. But they also still have Scottie Barnes, and he is delivering the young star goods as advertised. He is averaging 23.8 points, 7.4 rebounds, and 4.7 assists a night. On certain nights, he looks like the young superstar that represents his clearly attainable ceiling. On other nights, he and his team’s offense struggle and can’t seem to get unstuck from the mud. He’s doing a lot of things, but he isn’t doing it as efficiently or consistently as you’d like.

The real problems with the Raptors, though, lie elsewhere. Nobody can seemingly hit a three. RJ Barrett is getting to the line five times a game and hitting just 60% from the charity stripe. Collin Murray-Boyles has regressed, and Jakob Poeltl’s game has fallen off a cliff. It feels like if you solve Scottie, it helps you solve Barrett and Immanuel Quickley, and therefore, you solve the Raptors. Toronto has dropped six straight, and will be without the services of Barrett tonight.

Watching an Ausar Thompson and Scottie Barnes matchup could be electric. Barnes doesn’t have the defensive chops Ausar does, and Ausar doesn’t have the offensive versatility, but both could be liable to pull off a triple-double tonight. Cade Cunningham is also expected back tonight after sitting out Detroit’s win against the New Orleans Pelicans. Duncan Robinson and Ron Holland are out, and doubtful, respectively.

pistons.body:
DETROIT, MI - OCTOBER 16: Isaiah Joe #17 of the Detroit Pistons shoots the ball during the game against the Toronto Raptors on October 16, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Sevald/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Early season Fridays = NBA Cup day! The Detroit Pistons can climb to 2-0 in group play with a win over the worse-than-expected Toronto Raptors (1-1 in group play). The NBA thought this would’ve been a big game, handing out the Prime Video first game slot, but injuries, injuries, injuries.

Ron Holland, Duncan Robinson, and Jalen Duren are out again, but Cade Cunningham is expected to play. Injuries have slowed down the Raptors a ton.

RJ Barrett and Collin Murray-Boyles won’t suit up in Detroit. Kawhi Leonard remains out. His absence is the main source of Toronto’s struggle, but I still expected more.

GAME VITALS

Where: Little Caesars Arena, Detroit, MI

When: 7:30 PM ET

Watch: Prime Video

Odds: Pistons (-6.5)

The Raptors are still live even though they should be better. That said, Detroit isn’t a team that takes opponents lightly because of who’s in or out. The Pistons play the same brand of ball regardless of who’s out there on either side.

Wednesday’s 122-109 win over the New Orleans Pelicans tripled down on that point. Even a shorthanded Pistons squad without Cade manages to find a way.

Daniss Jenkins. Javonte Green. Ausar Thompson with the ball. Paul Reed with extended minutes — trustworthy things.

We got Isaiah Joe back in the lineup in that one! One of the marquee signings of Detroit’s offseason let it fly. Joe went 3-for-5 from range and put it on the floor, aiding Detroit’s flow. Bball Paul said Joe had more in his game during media day. Paul knows ball.

What do you know, it's Isaiah Joe

-Pistons able to flow into early offense with nothing there on initial push. DHO and now Joe gets a flare with an empty side
-Huerter cuts backdoor, pindown for Joe with an empty side. Turns the corner and the lob is there. pic.twitter.com/LZ8FQlRRAH
— Steve Jones (@stevejones20) November 19, 2026

The ability to leverage your shooting with live dribble decisions is an invaluable skill come playoff time. Love seeing Joe back out there, and more of that would be cool.

John Collins was on a heater (4-6 on 3s). He should get six 3s up every night with the room he has to fire. Collins will be matched up with Jakob Poeltl tonight. Poeltl is arguably the biggest hacker in the league. His 5.6 foul percentage ranks in the fourth percentile among bigs.

A lot of those Cade drives should end with trips to the charity stripe. Cade’s .37 FTr is a career high. He’s getting the calls and shooting ~86 percent at the line. That works. Cade is also putting together a strong All-Defense case, being a big-time contributor on the sixth-best defense.

Per Stathead, only Cade, Nikola Jokić, Matisse Thybulle, Scottie Barnes, and Caleb Wilson are averaging at least 0.9 blocks and 1.4 steals. Cade is doing this without fouling. He’s leveling up even more on that end.

Barnes recently declared himself the best defender in the world. I have no problem with that. He is up there. He’s a legit 1-5 defender. Anybody that good at something should feel they’re the best. That confidence got them where they are.

Barnes is Barnes, but I thought Toronto would have a more intimidating team defense. Cleaning The Glass ranks them 17th overall and 19th over the past two weeks + they are on a six-game losing streak.

The injury bug cannot be ignored, but I thought Toronto would be immune to long stretches of defensive lapses because of their suffocating gap principles.

Those principles still force turnovers at a frightening rate (2nd), but they haven’t dug in and clamped down like last year’s Raptors team. They’re still feisty enough to muddy up a game, but I expected more.

Toronto’s off-the-bounce creation takes a big blow with no Kawhi and Barrett. Barnes has more shot-making responsibilities this season. His 23.8 points per game are a career high. Immanuel Quickley will get them up. Catching fire vs. Ausar and the Pistons’ defense isn’t easy, but Toronto is looking to Quickley to provide immediate offense.

Jamison Battle is one of Toronto’s consistent snipers. He’s not a shooter you can disregard and is coming off a 19-point, 5-for-10 from 3 game. Ja’Kobe Walter can shoot it too and is quietly turning into a dependable heavy-minute wing.

With a win, Detroit could be in first or second in the East Group A division. The Orlando Magic (2-0) take on the struggling Brooklyn Nets (0-1) tonight. Should Orlando snag a win, they stay atop the group.

One game and one week at a time for Detroit in this tournament. They smacked around the Nets in their first cup game and look to do the same against the Raptors.

Projected starting lineup

Detroit Pistons (10-4): Cade Cunningham, Daniss Jenkins, Kevin Huerter, Ausar Thompson, John Collins

Toronto Raptors (5-10): Immanuel Quickley, Ja’Kobe Walter, Jamison Battle, Scottie Barnes, Jakob Poeltl

Question of the Day

The New York Knicks won the NBA Cup tourney and the real thing last year. Did that add any validity to the tournament?

pistons.headline: Pistons at Pelicans final score: No Cade, No Problem
pistons.body:
NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 18: Paul Reed #7 of the Detroit Pistons dunks in front of Karlo Matković #17 of the New Orleans Pelicans during the first half of a game at Smoothie King Center on November 18, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images

With as long as Detroit’s injury report has been recently, it got a little longer with Cade Cunningham as a late addition tonight. After the Pistons’ big win against San Antonio last night, it’s no surprise Deuce got some rest on the second night of a back-to-back.

JB Bickerstaff, with his shorthanded roster, rolled out the unusual starting lineup of Daniss Jenkins, Kevin Huerter, Javonte Green, Ausar Thompson, and John Collins. This would’ve been a great game for Ebuka Okorie to get some minutes, but he hurt his hip with the Motor City Cruise just the other day.

This meant Detroit’s key bench pieces were Paul Reed, Chaz Lanier, and Elijah Harkless. Even Tolu Smith saw some spot minutes when Collins and Reed both needed rest. Luckily, Isaiah Joe made his return to the lineup tonight after missing the last several games. Despite having to play guys from the end of the bench and on two-way spots, Detroit didn’t struggle against New Orleans.

Remember that unusual starting lineup for Detroit? Well, every single one of them finished in double digits. Jenkins, Green, and Collins all made at least three three-pointers. Jenkins, Thompson, and Huerter all had at least four assists, though Huerter had seven and DJ added nine.

Both Lanier and Joe made three three-pointers off the bench. Reed was the key sixth man once again, though that’s not all that peculiar nowadays. Harkless played his most minutes so far this season and did a great job sharing the rock with four assists.

In a game without their star player, this was another complete team win. There’s no doubt the depth on this team is one of the best in the league, and Detroit had seven different players score in double digits. Your Detroit Pistons are now 10-4 on the year.

Be sure you didn’t miss the lob finish by Woo:

— Detroit Pistons (@DetroitPistons) November 19, 2026

In an ultimate bit of disrespect, the Detroit Pistons are resting star Cade Cunningham tonight against the New Orleans Pelicans. The reasoning appears to be twofold — 1. Cunningham played last night. 2. The Pelicans. The poor, beleaguered Pelicans, home to former Pistons executives Joe Dumars and Troy Weaver, are not having a smooth go of it early in the season. They are 5-10, the coach is fighting with players, and a starter has already asked for a trade. That doesn’t mean there isn’t talent on the team. The Red Wings need to do everything in their power to make sure that the prospects are either drafted well or used effectively in trades.

lions.headline: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Bears in Week 12 on Thanksgiving
lions.body:
Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs (0) runs for a touchdown against Chicago Bears linebacker T.J. Edwards (53) during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 14, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Lions (8-2) and Chicago Bears (8-2) will face off at Ford Field in Detroit in a Week 12 showdown on Thanksgiving Day. With former Lions offensive coordinator Ben Johnson calling the shots in Chicago, it’s no surprise they mirror Detroit’s offense in several ways, and their recent success has certainly earned Lions coach Dan Campbell’s respect.

“They’re a lot like us. They play on the hunt, and they’re aggressive and run the football. And so this is a heck of a matchup. We’re looking forward to it.”

As strong as the Bears team has been over the past season and a half, going 15-2 against non-NFC North opponents, they’ve struggled against their rivals, producing a 2-6 record against the Lions, Packers, and Vikings. Johnson hasn’t beaten the Lions since leaving Detroit, and the last time he was at Ford Field, the Lions took it to him, winning 52-21. Expect Johnson to be motivated to change the narrative here.

This week’s prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, who currently have the Lions listed at +1900 to win this year’s Super Bowl and are currently 2.5-point underdogs in Week 12. Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will beat the Bucs in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint.

Bears base scheme

For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 12 preview: Breaking down the Bears’ offensive and defensive schemes.

Prediction 1: Lions find success on third down; win T.O.P.

Looking at the box score statistics, the Bears defense has some impressive numbers: 19.7 points allowed (6th best); 310.5 yards allowed per game (7th); and EPA per play: -0.15 (7th). But when you look closer at the efficiency rates, those numbers lose their luster. For example, their per-play numbers are in the bottom 10 in the NFL: EPA per play: 5.7 (28th); per pass: 7.7 (24th); and per run: 4.5 (25th).

The large disparity is mostly because the Bears’ defense has played the fewest snaps in the NFL (542). Chicago has been able to keep their defense on the sideline for two reasons: 1) Their offense holds the ball a league-leading 56.86% of the time; and 2) their defense gets off the field on 3rd down, allowing just a 26.6% conversion rate (Best in the NFL) and a third-down EPA allowed of -0.49 (2nd).

In the Bears’ most recent loss, the Packers succeeded in both categories, winning time of possession (30:24) and converting 4 of 12 (33%) on third down—and 1 of 1 on 4th down—though the real difference came by converting third downs in critical situations, earning a third-down EPA  of +0.25.

The Lions’ success on third down started off slow in 2026 but has steadily improved. Over their six-game winning streak, the Lions’ third-down success rate has ranged from 37-39%, but entering this game, it’s risen to nearly 42% for the season, after converting 7 of 11 (64%) with a +0.29 EPA on third down against the Bucs’ stout defense last week.

On third down this season, the Lions mainly lean on Amon-Ra St. Brown (38% target share), Jameson Williams (17%), and Jahmyr Gibbs (17%) in the passing game. Here’s a look at how each has performed on third downs this season:

St. Brown: 18 receptions on 31 targets for 243 yards (13.5 per) and 0.27 EPA per third-down target

Williams: 8 receptions on 14 targets for 145 yards (18.13 per) and 0.37 EPA per third-down target

Gibbs: 11 receptions on 14 targets for 114 yards (10.36 per) and 0.29 EPA per third-down target

Prediction 2: Lions lean into Gibbs early

One of the main ways the Lions will try to maintain possession is by establishing the run early. Jahmyr Gibbs currently leads the NFL with 1,098 rushing yards and 13 rushing touchdowns, plus 1,502 yards from scrimmage and 15 total touchdowns.

Again, the Bears’ box-score numbers make this look like a tough matchup. They are putting up top-10 numbers against the run: 94 run yards allowed per game (7th), a 39.6% success rate (6th), -0.1 EPA per rush allowed (8th), and 68 missed tackles (5th fewest in the NFL).

However, the Bears’ defensive efficiency numbers are once again on the other end of the spectrum, as they’re allowing 4.5 yards per rush (25th), 1.69 yards before contact (27th), and a 13.4% missed-tackle rate (25th); volume has been their biggest asset, and it could be their biggest enemy.

If the Bears don’t improve their tackle rate, Gibbs could give them problems all day. Here’s Next Gen Stats with more on Gibbs ‘ success in forcing missed tackles:

Jahmyr Gibbs has forced a league-high 92 missed tackles this season, 24 more than the next-closest player, Kenneth Walker (68). Those missed tackles have led to a league-high 496 yards after missed tackles, over 100 more than Jaylen Warren (388). That production has come consistently, as he has forced 10 or more missed tackles in four different games, the most in the NFL. The Bears have missed 13.4% of their tackle opportunities this season, the eighth-highest rate in the NFL.

Since the Bears acquired All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons, teams have slightly adjusted how they attack the Bears in the run game. The Seahawks, who faced Chicago in Simmons’ first game, ran inside on 53% of plays and were held below their season rushing average. The next week, the Bucs stayed away from inside runs (43%) and instead attacked the edge 57% of the time, rushing for 126 yards. Last Sunday, the Saints followed the Bucs’ strategy, attacked the edge on 55% of runs, and gained 120 yards on the ground (27 yards above their league average)

Look for the Lions to do the same. This season, the Lions attack the edge with outside runs on 54.6% of run plays (9th-highest rate), mainly leaning on an outside zone blocking scheme. According to Next Gen Stats, in these situations, Gibbs has gained 500 yards rushing, including 17 explosive run plays (best in the NFL), and has forced 43 missed tackles (best in the NFL).

Prediction 3: Exploit one-on-one matchups

While offenses have adjusted their approach with Simmons in the mix for the Bears, Chicago has adjusted its defense as well.

The Bears defensive coordinator, Dennis Allen, has historically run heavy man-coverage concepts (38-40% of the time), and while they started the season at that pace, they’ve since scaled things back and leaned more on zone concepts. Since the acquisition of Simmons, this has shifted even more, and over the last three games, the Bears have only run man coverage 22% of the time, while also leaning into more nickel sets (increasing from 59% to 70%) and two-high safety shells (up from 52% to 62%).

Essentially, with Simmons in the fold, the Bears are leaning into more four-man fronts and dropping seven into coverage to prevent big passing plays, and so far the results have been positive. Over the last three games, they’ve only allowed explosive plays on 5.2% of passing plays, the second-best mark in the NFL.

For the Lions passing offense to find success, they’ll need to do two things: 1) expose coverage with pre-snap diagnosis, and 2) be patient and take advantage of what the Bears are giving them.

Lions quarterback Jared Goff is one of the best in the NFL at reading defenses pre- and post-snap. He’s highly successful throwing against both man (EPA +0.52, 1st) and zone (+0.19, 8th) coverages, and has the skill players available to beat both.

St. Brown is Goff’s default option on most downs, especially on short and intermediate routes and in critical moments. In last year’s matchups, St. Brown dominated his one-on-ones against the Bears, catching 9 of 11 targets for 115 yards and 3 touchdowns in their first meeting, then securing 11 of 15 for 139 yards in their second.

But the Lions should also have an advantage deep, where Williams has been thriving lately. This season, when throwing deep, Goff has targeted Williams on half his attempts (12 attempts) and connected with him 67% of the time (8 receptions). According to Next Gen Stats, the Bears are allowing “45.7% completion percentage (7th-highest), 649 yards (2nd-most) and six touchdowns (tied-most) on deep passes this season.”

In last season’s matchups, Williams caught 2 of 4 targets for 108 yards and a touchdown, then followed it up by securing 6 of 8 targets for 74 yards in their second meeting. Expect another few deep shots in this game.

Prediction 4: Lions limit rushing attack, are opportunistic in secondary

While Caleb Williams will get all the national attention in this game, he’s been in a bit of a rut of late. Over the last three games, Williams has thrown for fewer than eight yards per pass attempt, along with five touchdowns and five interceptions. In the one game he exceeded 250 yards passing, his passer rating was just 61.5 because of turnovers—four interceptions to the Bucs’ defense.

With Williams’ play a bit erratic, look for the Lions to work hard to limit the Bears’ rushing attack. And like on defense, the box score numbers look a lot better than their efficiency stats due to volume:

Rush yards per attempt: 4.2 (14th); EPA per rush: -0.06 (16th)

Explosive runs over last four games: 5.3% (31st in the NFL)

Runs of 10+ yards: 29 on season (13th) — only six in the last four games

Success rate over last four games: 40.8% (16th)

Rush yards over expectations: -27 (20th)

If the Lions can slow down the Bears’ run game, Williams tends to try to force the issue. Williams is a dynamic athlete with an uncanny ability to extend plays and keep his options open, but he has tended—especially over the last three weeks—to try and force big plays instead of taking easier checkdowns, leading to mistakes and turnovers.

Last Sunday, after the Lions beat the Bucs, Kerby Joseph said he was disappointed he didn’t secure an interception on his return because Baker Mayfield wasn’t willing to test them deep. The Lions won’t have that problem with Williams, so Joseph will likely get an opportunity to get his hands on one in this game.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions vs. Chicago Bears preview, prediction: On Paper
lions.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 14: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions looks on at the line of scrimmage against the Chicago Bears at Ford Field on September 14, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The 8-2 Detroit Lions face the 8-2 Chicago Bears face off on Thursday for one of the most anticipated Thanksgiving Day matchups in recent history.

The NFC North lead is on the line, but which team holds the advantage? Let’s take a closer look in our Lions vs. Bears preview and prediction: On Paper.

Lions pass offense (8th in DVOA) vs. Bears pass defense (10th)

My season-long faith in the Lions’ passing attack was awarded last week when I gave Detroit the advantage despite the Bucs’ pass defense (3rd) ranking significantly higher than Detroit’s (11th) in DVOA. Based on all the evidence, I still believe DVOA hasn’t caught up to Detroit’s true efficiency through the air, although they are getting closer now. For the season, Detroit’s passing attack ranks:

Fourth in passer rating (107.8)

Fourth in yards per attempt (8.2)

Third in dropback EPA (0.217)

Third in dropback success rate (52.5%)

By nearly all accounts, this is a top-five passing attack, and it feels like the only time they’ve really been slowed down is a weird game against the Dolphins (I blame Christian Mahogany’s benching) and against the unique Vikings defense. Last week’s dominance against the Buccaneers only strengthened my resolve that this unit is nearly unstoppable, and they may be getting better.

Pass protection is pretty darn solid, and that’s going to be important this week against a surging Bears defensive line. Detroit ranks fourth in ESPN’s pass block win rate, second in PFF pass blocking grade, and ninth in pressure rate allowed.

The Bears’ pass defense has been pretty up and down this year, but my eye is immediately drawn to the last three games. They’ve shut down the Seahawks, Bucs, and Saints—admittedly not great passing offenses—but it’s hard not to connect that with the recent addition of Jeffery Simmons, who has been an absolute monster in the last three games. In his short time with the Bears, he already has five sacks and two pass breakups. But the Lions’ offensive line and passing attack will be Chicago’s biggest defensive test they’ve faced since at least the Patriots—maybe all season.

Chicago’s season-long averages are good but not great:

17th in passer rating allowed (89.8)

25th in yards per attempt (7.7)

Seventh in dropback EPA (-0.036)

Fifth in dropback success rate (41.9%)

It’s an odd split of stats, seeing them so pedestrian in basic statistics, but nearly elite in advanced stats. I think there are two reasons for this disconnect. One, I think Chicago may be giving up a fair amount of garbage time stats. When we only account for data when the win percentage is between 5-95% (a very small cutting out of garbage time stats), Chicago’s pass defense jumps to second in EPA and second in success rate.

Additionally, the Bears create a ton of disruptive plays. Again, they are near the top of the league in interception (eight, t-10th), and they’re also fourth in sacks (32). But if you can pass protect and take care of the ball, there is some vulnerability here. The Lions are pretty darn good at doing both of those things.

Player to watch: Simmons. I don’t think you can overstate his impact on the game. It’s not just Simmons being unstoppable, but he’s made his surrounding cast much better. Montez Sweat has 12 pressures in three games since Simmons was back, Grady Jarrett has nine, and Austin Booker has 11.

Advantage: Lions +1.5. The Bears believe they can create pressure with just four players now, which has helped a struggling secondary. I’m not so sure Chicago can get away with that this week. They’ll create some issues, and it’ll be important for Jared Goff to take care of the football. However, it feels like the Lions have answers for everything the Bears do well in this matchup.

Lions run offense (1st) vs. Bears run defense (18th)

Detroit’s running game wasn’t flashy against the Buccaneers, but it was effective. The Lions were able to consistently stay ahead of the sticks despite going up against the best run defense in football, and eventually they broke through with a few explosives late in the game to seal the win.

That performance should give you confidence the Lions can run against just about anybody. It really feels like they’ve found answers since that Vikings game.

For the year, Detroit ranks:

Ninth in yards per carry (4.5)

Eighth in rush EPA (0.003)

Third in success rate (49.6%)

And since that Vikings game?

Seventh in yards per carry (4.9)

Fourth in rush EPA (0.106)

Third in success rate (51.1%)

And mind you in those four weeks, the Lions have faced two of the best run defenses in football (Vikings and Bucs).

All of that is to say I’m pretty darn confident in this rushing attack right now. The offensive line is coming together, as evidenced by their rank in adjusted line yards (second), run-block win rate (fourth), and PFF run-block grade (fourth).

It’s hard to get a handle on the Bears’ run defense because they haven’t faced a lot of runs this season. Because they haven’t been trailing in a game since October 11, Chicago has faced a league-low 207 attempts (next lowest is 230). But in terms of down-to-down efficiency, they actually aren’t that good. They rank:

25th in yards per carry allowed (4.5)

12th in rush EPA (-0.064)

14th in rush success rate (41.2%)

But there is something that they do really excel at and that’s short-yardage situations. They’re allowing conversions on just 47% of those situations, which is the second-best mark in the NFL. That’s something the Lions struggled with early in the season, but have improved at significantly as of late. For the year, Detroit is now converting on 74% of power runs, sixth-highest.

Digging deeper, I’m not all that impressed by the Bears’ statistical marks. They’re 27th in run-stop win rate, 31st in PFF run-defense grade, and 18th in adjusted line yards. Simmons certainly helps, but this feels like a weakness that Chicago has been able to hide well because of game script.

Player to watch: Austin Booker. The third-year Bears defensive end is having a solid season, and his 76.8 run-defense grade is ninth-best among edge defenders. But he mostly lines up opposite the left tackle. So we’ll see how he fares against Penei Sewell.

Advantage: Lions +2. My confidence has never been higher in the Lions’ run game, and while Chicago hasn’t allowed more than 126 rushing yards in a game, I think that’s a mirage caused by facing mostly poor rushing attacks and forcing teams to abandon the run game by getting out to early leads.

Bears pass offense (12th) vs. Lions pass defense (21st)

Bold and italicized data indicate games in which Caleb Williams was out

There’s been ups and downs in Caleb Williams’ third NFL season, but far more ups than downs. Let’s compare his statline from last year to this year:

2025: 58.1% completion percentage, 6.9 Y/A, 27 TDs, 7 INTs, 90.1 passer rating
2026: 68.3% completion percentage, 7.9 Y/A, 10 TDs, 6 INTs, 95.9 passer rating

He’s been more accurate, deadlier down the field, and while the interceptions are up, that’s largely the result of a single four-interception outing against the Bucs.

For the season, the Bears rank:

19th in passer rating (88.8)

14th in yards per attempt (7.4)

13th in dropback EPA (0.089)

Sixth in success rate (51.5%)

Another big difference between 2025 and 2026 Williams is the deep shot. Last year, he was uncorking a deep shot 10.6% of the time. That’s down to just 8.3% this year, as he’s learned to better take what the defense is giving him. His average depth of target is slightly down, too, dropping from 8.5 to 8.2.

Some of the mediocre stats are the result of a three-game stretch without Williams. But there are some underlying issues, too. Most notably, the pass protection has taken a small step back from last year.

But where the passing game has struggled is pass protection. One of the best units last year, the Bears rank just 11th in PFF’s pass-blocking grade, 22nd in pressure rate, but sixth in pass-block win rate. Williams has been expertly evading pressure and extending plays, but with his early-season hamstring injury, it appears that skill has taken a step back: he’s endured 16 sacks in just seven games.

Still, I believe this to be close to a top-10 passing attack with a ton of extraordinary pass-catchers in Rome Odunze, Luther Burden, Colston Loveland, and Kalif Raymond.

The Lions defense has slowly been pulling themselves out of the basement of the NFL, but this chart shows why there’s still some reason for healthy skepticism about the pass defense. They were great against the Packers and Dolphins, but I’m not ready to give them too much credit for the Patriots game after Drake Maye went down in the first quarter.

That said, the season-long stats are starting to look much better:

19th in passer rating allowed (94.8)

13th in yards per attempt (6.9)

26th in dropback EPA (0.127)

24th in success rate (48.8%)

How will they look against a more competent offense this week? How will they respond to the losses of Aidan Hutchinson, Skyler Gill-Howard, and Jack Campbell? We don’t have great answers to these questions right now, but at the very least, I think we can somewhat comfortably say they’re better than they were in the first month of the season.

But pass rush may be a growing concern, especially in this game. In addition to the defensive losses above, DJ Wonnum has not practiced yet this week, and Detroit’s pass rush has been slowing down steadily as the season has gone on. Back in Week 4, the Lions had the eighth highest pressure rate (39.3%). Now they’re down to 37.0% on the year (14th).

Part of that is a significant drop in blitz rate, but I wonder if Detroit will consider upping the blitz rate moving forward. They have more stability in the secondary with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph back, so the pass rush could use some extra oomph. Plus, Caleb Williams is a much different quarterback vs. the blitz:

Williams vs. blitz: 19th in EPA/dropback

No blitz: 4th EPA/dropback

Player to watch: Coleston Loveland vs. Brian Branch. Detroit has struggled all season in defending tight ends (76.2 yards per game, third-most), and Loveland is 10th among tight ends in receptions. But Branch’s return gives the Lions a defensive weapon in the slot.

Advantage: Bears +2. I’m still pretty nervous about the Lions’ pass defense, particularly as the injuries start to mount. Pass rush has quietly been a growing concern, and that could be even more pronounced this week with Hutchinson, Gill-Howard, and DJ Wonnum all possibly out. I do hope the Lions dial up the aggression, but I don’t know yet if Detroit’s back end is improved enough to handle the extra pressure.

Bears run offense (15th) vs. Lions run defense (20th)

One of the biggest surprises in my research this week was finding that Chicago’s rushing attack had taken a massive step back this year. Last year, they ranked third in DVOA and sixth in EPA. This year, they rank:

14th in yards per carry (4.2)

14th in rush EPA (-0.043)

20th in success rate (39.9%)

The loss of center Drew Dalman has undoubtedly served as a primary reason for the regression. As a team, the Bears rank just 22nd in run-block win rate, but eighth in adjusted line yards, and third in PFF run-blocking grade. They’re still very dangerous running the ball to the right side of the line, where right tackle Darnell Wright and right guard Jonah Jackson are still having fantastic success—but the left side is a liability.

Detroit’s run defense took a big step toward legitimacy last week, shutting down Bucky Irving and the Buccaneers for most of the game. They haven’t allowed a 100-yard rusher since Chuba Hubbard in Week 4, and they’ve held four of their last six opponents below 4.0 yards per carry. For the season, Detroit ranks:

14th in yards per carry allowed (4.0)

10th in rush EPA (-0.069)

10th in rush success  rate (40.0%)

After some early-season struggles, the Lions have seemingly righted the ship—and not against terrible opponents, either.

Overall, Detroit, oddly, ranks 26th in run-stop win rate, but third in adjusted line yards, seventh in run defense PFF grade, 14th in stuffed rate, and first in yards after contact per rush.

Player to watch: K.J. Britt. Britt just joined the Lions defense a few weeks ago, but he’s already made several impact plays on defense, particularly in the run game. Both him and Malcolm Rodriguez have done an excellent job filling in for Jack Campbell.

Advantage: Lions +1. I think the Lions could absolutely shut down the Bears’ rushing attack this week. While there is a concern that Ben Johnson mixes things up and throws some effective misdirection at Detroit, the Lions have been much more disciplined than they were earlier in the season.

Last week’s prediction:

I certainly underestimated just how effective the Lions’ passing attack would be against the Bucs, even if I had a sneaking suspicion it could happen. Everything else was pretty much on point. But, again, I missed badly on the final score. On Paper is now 8-2 overall, but just 4-6 against the spread.

In the comment section, we had a lot of very close guesses, but nobody was closer than Lee County Flydog with their 31-20 prediction. They also predicted a statline for Jared Goff that wasn’t too far off from the real thing:

Prediction: 31-37, 324 yards, 3 TDs
Actual: 20-28, 279 yards, 2 TDs

I also want to give shout outs to MATH2010 and Deb in Co, they both predicted 31-14 Lions, which would’ve been the score had Tampa not added a garbage time touchdown with eight seconds left.

Alas, the prize goes to Lee County Flydog. Enjoy.

This week’s prediction:

Call me crazy, but I think this is a better matchup for the Lions than last week’s game against the Buccaneers. Detroit has a +3.5 advantage against the Bears, and the edge in three of the four matchups.

I respect the Bears, but there are some underlying concerns about their defense and run game. The Jeffery Simmons hype has been warranted, but it also is masking over some poor play elsewhere on defense. I think the Lions can exploit that.

The only thing that gives me serious pause in this matchup is timing. The Lions are coming off an exhaustive three-game stretch and have lost three critical defensive players in the last four games. Meanwhile, the Bears are just a week removed from their bye week, and some Chicago fans believe their focus has been on this game for a while.

But we rarely see a Dan Campbell team not up for the fight. Lions 34, Bears 27.

lions.headline: Lions vs. Bears 5 Qs preview: Is Caleb Williams an MVP candidate?
lions.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 04: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears scrambles to throw while pressured by Rock Ya-Sin #23 of the Detroit Lions in the second quarter at Soldier Field on January 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images

It’s a Thanksgiving Day matchup that no one will soon forget: the Detroit Lions (8-2) will take on the Chicago Bears (8-2) from Ford Field for the sole spot atop the NFC North.

We had the pleasure of connecting with Bill Zimmerman, Deputy Editor of Windy City Gridiron, to give us some insight into this Chicago squad ahead of Thursday afternoon’s divisional tilt. We learned about Caleb Williams’ Year 3 leap into the top-10 quarterback conversation, what’s behind the sudden regression of Chicago’s rushing attack, and how injuries in the secondary have forced Dennis Allen into heavier base looks—plus how trade-deadline acquisition Jeffery Simmons has transformed the Bears’ defensive front into a top-10 unit.

1. Last week, Mike Florio and Chris Simms talked about Caleb Williams’ chances at being the league’s MVP, with Florio claiming Williams “would be one of the top MVP candidates right now if he hadn’t missed those three games,” and Simms stating that Caleb has “injected himself into the conversation of the best quarterback in the NFL.”

Do you agree with these bold proclamations? If so, where in Williams’ game have you seen him make the leap to becoming an elite quarterback? In what areas do you think he still has room to grow in Year 3?

Alright, so let’s play this out. Caleb never gets hurt. What is the Bears record? There’s a good chance they win the game against Minnesota. Caleb was literally going in for the go ahead score when he hurt his hamstring. What would have happened against Green Bay? Hard to say, but let’s say they lose that game in a far more competitive football game.

If the Bears are 9-1 right now with Caleb doing some of the things he’s done on national television, I do think he would be in the MVP conversation. However, if I’m being fully objective, 4 interceptions on Sunday Night Football followed up by a subpar performance against the New Orleans Saints would have derailed any hope he would have at the MVP in 2026.

That being said, I do think Caleb has taken significant strides and is playing outstanding football. Since he’s returned from injury, the Bears have literally not trailed for 1 second in a football game. That’s since October 11th. Caleb hasn’t trailed in a football game since September 20th. He’s operating in structure very well, his completion percentage (what everyone loved to complain about last year) is now 3rd in the league, and he still has the ability to make absurd throws on the move with incredible accuracy and velocity on the football.

So do I think Caleb is an MVP candidate, even if he was healthy? No. But I do think Caleb is pushing to be one of the top 5 QBs in the league and could get there if he plays well down the stretch against strong competition. I think he should be considered one of the top 10 QBs in the league right now.

2. Chicago’s run game was one of their biggest strengths a year ago, ranking fourth in EPA/rush and second in rush success rate. This season, the Bears rank 17th in EPA/rush and 16th in rush success rate.

How much of that slide back to being an average rushing attack has to do with Kyle Monangai’s extended absence? D’Andre Swift is averaging just 3.7 yards per carry, down from 4.9 yards per carry a season ago, and his success rate this year (48.8%) has taken a hit as well, down from 54.7% in 2025. How much of this is on the running backs, how much of this has to do with the offensive line, and how much of it has had to do with matchups or quality of opponent?

Your guess on the run game is as good as mine, and honestly, maybe Ben Johnson. The running game has not been nearly as strong this year even though it’s still a point of emphasis. Kyle Monangai being out certainly hurt, but he was back against the Saints last week and people (Tom Brady included) were expecting a big leap forward and it didn’t happen.

If the Bears are going to be a true Super Bowl contender this year, they need to figure out the running game and get it closer to the 2025 version than what it’s largely been in 2026. They’ve shown the ability to run it just as well earlier in the year, but they haven’t been firing the last few weeks.

Perhaps it’s that the offensive line isn’t quite as strong this year. Darnell Wright and Jonah Jackson are still a dynamite run-blocking duo on the right side, but Joe Thuney might be showing his age, he’s still good but not elite like last season and Drew Dalman’s surprise retirement forcing them to go to Garrett Bradbury has been a significant downgrade at center.

Either way, as Lions fans, you know how important the run game is to Ben Johnson and he’s still going to be focused on making sure it’s working as we go down the stretch here in the regular season.

3. Chicago’s defense has undergone some pretty dramatic changes from a year ago in terms of personnel deployment. Last year, the Bears lined up in base just 12.6% of the time, the third-lowest rate in the NFL. In 2026, the Bears find themselves in base on 33.8% of snaps, the eighth-highest clip in the league.

What changes to Chicago’s roster dictated this shift to more base personnel? How much of this scheme change has helped the Bears defense improve this season, going from 19th in EPA/play to seventh?

Honestly, the biggest thing that happened were injuries and issues in their secondary. The Bears planned on having a secondary of rookie Dillon Thieneman and Coby Bryant at safety and Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson at outside corners and Kyler Gordon at nickel.

Coby Bryant went down in August and hasn’t played yet, that’s forced backup Nickel Cam Lewis to play a lot of safety. Kyler Gordon also missed a ton of time as well, and the other backup nickel, rookie Malik Muhammad was already playing outside because Tyrique Stevenson has been hurt and ineffective when he’s been healthy.

I think Dennis Allen has just realized that until his secondary is healthier and playing better, putting their third linebacker, D’Marco Jackson, on the field, who’s decent in coverage as is, was a better option than whatever was left in their secondary room.

4. The Bears took a huge swing at the trade deadline, acquiring Jeffery Simmons to hold things down in the middle of their defense. The pressures and the sacks were a given, but in what other ways have you noticed Simmons making an impact for Chicago’s defense that maybe you weren’t expecting?

Jeffery Simmons has elevated the entire Bears defense from a liability to a top-ten unit in the league. Yes, Simmons is making an impact on the stat sheet. But how he’s elevated everyone else on the D is incredible. Montez Sweat is playing his best football since 2023. Grady Jarrett hasn’t been great since becoming a Bear last year, he’s much better. Austin Booker at the other edge is making impact plays. Devin Bush was brought in as a free agent and he’d been bogged down with blockers the first several games, but now he’s running free and making big plays. Not only that, the Bears are now getting pressure with 4 and Dennis Allen doesn’t have to blitz nearly as much so that’s more bodies to drop back in a weak secondary, and pressure is getting home quicker so they don’t have to cover as long.

Not only that, but Simmons is already a leader in the locker room both vocally and by example. This is one of the great midseason acquisitions I can ever remember and probably the best one in the history of the Chicago Bears.

5. The Bears opened as 2.5-point favorites over at FanDuel Sportsbook heading into this Thanksgiving Day matchup against the Lions. What’s one thing you want to see, what’s one thing you need to see, and one thing you’re sure you’ll see happen in this matchup between the Lions and Bears on Thursday?

I’ve never had this question posed to me this way. That’s interesting and makes me think. Good one.

The one thing I want to see is how this Jeffery Simmons-led defense does against an elite offense like the Lions. They haven’t played a spectacular offense with Simmons and I am very curious to see how this new defense looks against a talented offense.

The one thing I need to see is that the Bears running game starts looking better, because if it does, they are going to be really hard to beat.

The one thing I’m sure we will see is that this is going to be a great game on Thursday. I think the Lions will score some points, as will the Bears, but I do think if the Bears running game looks like it has the last couple of weeks, the offense won’t click and the Lions will win. If the Bears running game gets back on track, I do think the Bears can go into Detroit and win this one.

I’ll say Lions win this 24-20 based on how the Bears offense has looked the last two games. But if the offense clicks, the Ben Johnson and the Bears are going to keep the gas to the floor.
