lions.headline: Lions Week 12 preview: Breaking down Bears’ offensive, defensive schemes
lions.body:
Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images | Getty Images

In Week 12, the Detroit Lions (8-2) and Chicago Bears (8-2) will square off in a Thanksgiving Day showdown at Ford Field, with the NFC North’s top spot on the line. For the second week in a row, Lions coach Dan Campbell is very familiar with the opponent’s coaching staff: the Bears are led by former Lions offensive coordinator Ben Johnson, along with several other former Lions coaches, and a few individuals he coached alongside in New Orleans.

“Obviously got a real good opponent coming up. It’s a hot team, 8-2 like we are. A division opponent. Ben (Johnson)’s done a hell of a job out there, so has (Bears Defensive Coordinator Dennis Allen) DA. I mentioned this before, I know a lot of those coaches, obviously we had them on staff here and then a lot of coaches that I coached with at New Orleans when I was there, (Bears Offensive line coach) Dan Roushar, O-line coach, certainly DA. So, got a lot of respect for what they do out there.”

Let’s take a closer look at the Bears’ coaching staff, the scheme that they run, and some scouting notes from previously viewed games.

Bears head coach: Ben Johnson

NFL coaching seasons: 15th season (Bears, Lions, Dolphins)
Head coaching seasons: Second (Bears 2025-present)
Offensive coordinator seasons: Three (Lions 2022-24)
Influences: Dan Campbell, Zac Taylor, Darrell Bevell, Mike Martz, Adam Gase, Mike Sherman, Bill Lazor
Coached under: Campbell, Matt Patricia, Gase, Joe Philbin
Playcaller: Yes

Since Bears coach Ben Johnson left the Lions for the Chicago’s head coaching job, he’s taken the league by storm, but has surprisingly struggled against the NFC North. Against non-NFC North opponents, Johnson’s Bears are 15-2, but against division rivals, Chicago is just 2-6, including losses to the Lions both times they’ve played and a 52-21 loss the last time he was in Ford Field. Expect Johnson to be motivated to change the narrative this week.

Offensive coordinator: Press Taylor

NFL coaching seasons: 14 seasons (Bears, Jaguars, Colts, Eagles)
Offensive coordinator seasons: Fourth (Bears 2026, Jaguars 2022-24)
Previous positions held: Passing game coordinator (Bears 2025, Eagles 2020), QB coach, Offensive assistant, Assistant QB coach, quality control
Influences: Zac Taylor (Bengals HC, brother), Ben Johnson, Doug Pederson, Frank Reich, Chip Kelly
Coached under: Johnson, Pederson, Reich, Kelly
Lions ties to coaching staff: Antwaan Randle El (WR coach), J.T. Barrett (QB coach)

Offensive scheme

Passing game: Ben Johnson’s West Coast, Modern Pro-style scheme
Running scheme: Multiple, Gap and Outside zone
Staples of scheme:

Primarily 11 personnel (50% on the season, 56% over last four games)

They use 12 personnel more than 90% of the NFL (33% on the season, 30% over last four)

13 personnel has been scaled back a bit (16.6% season, 13% last four) but still above 80% of teams

Core values: Strive for run-pass balance (55-45 split), heavy play action (36%, most in the NFL), pre-snap motion, bunch formations, YAC (9th most in NFL), screens, gadget plays, trick plays, willing to run on any down and distance, not scared to go for it on 4th down (58% success rate, 13th)

Put points and yards on the board: 26.2 per game (8th); 375.8 yards per game (8th)

Strive to control the ball/clock with time of possession: 56.86% (best in NFL)

QB Caleb Williams is willing to hold on to the ball to try and make a big play

Passing explosives in last four games: 12.7% (third best in the NFL)

Passer rating is slightly above average: 95.9 (12th)

Williams EPA per dropback: +0.15 (11th)

Solid vs. Zone coverage (EPA: +0.11, 13th), but below average vs. Man coverage (EPA: -0.01, 26th)

Teams blitz Williams at the highest rate in the NFL (49%); for good reason (EPA: -0.03, 22nd)

Williams scramble skill keep pressure/sacks low: 19th in pressures, 22nd in rate; 12th in sacks and rate

Rome Odunze is the deep shot receiver: EPA: 50.23; Target share: 17.5%

Luther Buren is a volume/consistent receiver: EPA: 31.36; Target share: 22%

TE Colston Loveland = volume/consistent: EPA: 26.82; Target share: 19%

Run game is heavy outside zone (54% of runs); Outside runs 61% of the time (4th most)

Run game numbers can be deceiving if you only look at the box score: 142.4 per-game average (3rd)

The rest of the numbers are average at best

Rush yards per attempt: 4.2 (14th); EPA per rush: -0.06 (16th)

Explosive runs over last four games: 5.3% (31st in the NFL)

Runs of 10+ yards: 29 on season (13th) — only six in the last four games

Success rate over last four games: 40.8% (16th)

Rush yards over expectations: -27 (20th)

Dan Campbell on the Bears’ offense:

“They’re finding ways to win. (QB) Caleb (Williams), he’s a heck of a player, man. Dynamic. And they have got weapons, man. (WR Luther) Burden’s having a big year. (TE) Colston (Loveland), the O-line’s playing well. They’ve been able to stay intact, play together. (RB D’Andre) Swift’s having a good year and they got (RB Kyle Monangai) 25 back. Certainly know (WR Kalif Raymond) Leaf very well. (WR Rome) Odunze, that whole deal.”

Defensive Coordinator: Dennis Allen

NFL coaching seasons: 25th season
Head coaching seasons: Six (Saints 2022-24, Raiders 2012-14)
Defensive coordinator seasons: 10th (Bears 2025-present, Saints 2015-21, Broncos 2011)
Previous roles: Senior assistant, secondary coach, Assistant DL coach, Defensive assistant, quality control
Influences: Sean Payton, Gregg Williams, John Fox, Jim L. Mora Jr., and Dan Reeves
Coached under: Ben Johnson, Payton, Jack Del Rio, Fox, Mora Jr.,  Reeves

Defensive scheme

Base: 4-2, attacking 1-gapping front
Coverage: Bump-and-run, press-man coverage
Staples of scheme:

For the season, the Bears use Nickel 60% of the time, with Base 34%, and DIME 6%

Since acquiring DT Jeffery Simmons, things have shifted a bit more toward coverage

Last three games with Simmons in mix: Nickel 70% of the time, Base 27%, and DIME 3%

There has also been a heavier shift from Man to Zone coverage and single-high to two-high sets

ZONE: 69% for the season, 77% over the last three games

Two-high shell: 52% for the season, 62% over the last three games

Results show up in explosive passing plays allowed: 5.2% (2nd best over last three games)

On paper, the box score numbers are very good

19.7 points allowed (6th best); 310.5 yards allowed per game (7th); EPA per play: -0.15 (7th)

Some of this is because they have the fewest plays against: 542 (fewest in the NFL)

However, yards allowed per play: 5.7 (28th); per pass: 7.7 (24th); per run: 4.5 (25th)

Hasn’t hurt them overall because they get off the field on 3rd down: 26.6% conversion rate allowed (1st)

Historically, have preferred to rush four with DL stunts

But have introduced more blitzing in 2026 (35.1%, 10th most) – Double mug (A-gap)

Good anticipation of offensive tendencies against blitz

Pressures are average: 132 (19th); rate: 37.7% (11th)

Sacks are above-average: 32 (4th); rate: 9.1% (2nd)

Prioritize stopping the run as a principle

Solid overall box score numbers: 94 run yards allowed per game (7th); success rate: 39.6% (6th)

Susceptible to explosive runs: 10.5% (17th) and yards before contact: 1.69 (27th)

Dan Campbell on the Bears’ defense:

“And then defensively, man, they’re playing really good, man. It’s just to continue to grow another year in the system. (DT Jeffery) Simmons is a heck of a player, always has been. That was a good addition for them. (DT) Grady (Jarrett)’s a good player. (EDGE Montez) Sweat. I think (EDGE Austin) Booker has even upped his game in some of the stuff at the overhang and getting (LB Devin) Bush has been big for them, linebacker position. And they have got the corners, (CB) Jaylon (Johnson) and (CB Tyrique) Stevenson over there.”

lions.headline: Former Detroit Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford dies at age 101
lions.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 24: Detroit Lions Head Coach Dan Campbell talks with Detroit Lions Owner/Chair Emeritus Martha Firestone Ford during pregame prior to the Detroit Lions versus the Green Bay Packers game on Sunday November 6, 2022 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

The Detroit Lions announced on Tuesday night that former team owner Martha Firestone Ford has passed away at age 101. According to the team, she passed away at her home surrounded by family.

Ford took over as principal owner of the franchise in 2014, following the death of her husband, William Clay Ford. She held onto the role until 2020, when she bequeathed primary ownership to her daughter and current Lions owner Sheila Hamp.

Since then, Ford has been serving as Owner/Chair Emeritus of the team. Here’s how the team described her role over the past six years.

In her most recent role as Owner/Chair Emeritus, Mrs. Ford supported her four children – Principal Owner/Chair Sheila Ford Hamp, Owner/Vice Chair Martha Ford Morse, Owner/Vice Chair William Clay Ford Jr., and Owner/Vice Chair Elizabeth Ford Kontulis – as they assumed leadership responsibilities within the family franchise. Today the Ford family proudly carries forward the legacy established by Mr. and Mrs. Ford, preserving the values, love, and passion that have shaped a family tradition spanning multiple generations.

During Mrs. Ford’s brief stint as primary owner, the Lions made the playoffs twice (2014, 2016) and produced three winning seasons.

The team offered this official statement on Ford’s passing:

“It is with heavy hearts that we acknowledge the passing of Martha Firestone Ford. Mrs. Ford inspired us all as a pillar of the Detroit community and the passionate matriarch of the Detroit Lions football team.

“She will always be remembered for her fierce loyalty to her family, her community, and the city of Detroit.

“Her presence on our sideline, in our building, and in our community will be greatly missed. We wish the entire Ford and Firestone families peace in this time of mourning.”

For more on Mrs. Ford’s passing and her life accomplishments, check out the Detroit Lions’ official story.

lions.headline: Lions, Bears Week 12 injury report: Sam LaPorta, Chuck Clark upgraded on Tuesday
lions.body:
Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta (87) makes a catch against Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Lions (8-2) and Chicago Bears (8-2) will square off in this year’s Thanksgiving Day battle, and for the second straight day, the Lions and Bears have opted for walkthrough practices.

A walkthrough practice means that all participation levels are estimates from the coaching staff based on how the player would have participated in a traditional practice. So, with that in mind, let’s look at Tuesday’s injury report and get you up to date on what we know.

Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded

Estimated no practice

DT Skyler Gill-Howard (knee) — Update: His season is over

EDGE DJ Wonnum (back)

CB Ennis Rakestraw (shoulder)

Gill-Howard’s knee injury is significant enough to require surgery and will end his rookie season. A staple of the Lions’ three-man interior defensive line, the Lions will need more production from their depth players beyond starters Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams.

“Sky is out for the year. He has a knee injury that will require surgery, so he’ll be out. I hate that for him. He’s had a heck of a season up until this point,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Tuesday. Later adding, “He’s done a really good job for us. But we’ve still got Mac (McNeill), we still have Tyleik, we’ve still got Levi (Onwuzurike), we’ve got (Tyler) Lacy that can play in there. Could see (Mekhi) Wingo. We’ve got options there, but you hate to lose a player like him. He’s had a heck of a rookie season.”

Wonnum played a full allotment of snaps last Sunday, but his injury appeared to pop up afterward and is significant enough to make him a game-time decision on Thursday, per Campbell. New injuries can be brutal on a short week, but there’s still room for optimism.

Rakestraw’s injury kept him out of last weekend’s game, so starting the week with continued restrictions isn’t a great sign for his availability. Campbell didn’t say it directly, but he’ll likely be a game-time decision, too.

Estimated limited practice

S Chuck Clark (hamstring) — Upgraded from No Practice

Clark, like Wonnum, didn’t have a notable injury during Sunday’s game but was estimated to have missed practice on Monday. While it’s an encouraging sign to see him upgraded for Tuesday’s practice, he is also expected to be a game-time decision.

Estimated full practice

TE Sam LaPorta (ankle) — Upgraded from Limited

CB D.J. Reed (hip)

CB Khalil Dorsey (wrist)

LaPorta was estimated to have been limited on Monday, but would have gotten in a full practice on Tuesday if it had been a traditional practice day. That’s a great sign for his availability on Thursday.

Reed continues to improve, but with the Lions taking a slow approach to his recovery, despite the estimated full practices, he’s still likely to be a game-time decision, per Campbell:

“Yeah, he’s improving. I mean, I thought he ran around pretty good yesterday. But I can’t give a definitive answer on that just yet. Probably come down, could be game time decision.”

Dorsey was injured in the game but returned and played snaps on special teams. With an estimated full practice under his belt, he appears to have a good chance to play on Thursday.

Bears’ injury report

Estimated did not practice

RB Roschon Johnson (ankle) — injured last game

CB Kyler Gordon (shoulder) — missed last game

S Elijah Hicks (concussion) — NEW INJURY

Estimated full practice

LT Theo Benedet (quad) — Upgraded from did not practice on Monday

LB D’Marco Jackson (elbow)

lions.headline: Detroit Lions lose another defender to season-ending injury
lions.body:
DETROIT,MICHIGAN-NOVEMBER 22: Defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard (50) of the Detroit Lions looks on from the sidelines during an NFL football game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, November 22, 2026. (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images

The injuries to the Detroit Lions defense are starting to mount. On Tuesday, Lions coach Dan Campbell revealed that rookie defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard is out for the rest of the season with a knee injury sustained during the team’s win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday. Campbell said the injury occurred when Gill-Howard was in the game during a goal-line play on offense.

“Sky is out for the year. He’s out for the year. He had a knee injury that will require surgery. So he’ll be out,” Campbell said. “I hate that for him. He’s had a heck of a season up to this point.”

It’s the third significant injury to a Lions defender in the past four weeks, joining linebacker Jack Campbell (neck) and Aidan Hutchinson (torn ACL).

Gill-Howard, the team’s sixth-round pick this year, was one of the most pleasant surprises from Detroit’s defense this year. He’s played 316 defensive snaps through 10 games, tallying 2.0 sacks, six quarterback hits, and a tackle for loss.

His loss, combined with Hutchinson’s season-ending injury, leaves the Lions a bit shorthanded on the defensive line in terms of pass rushers, but Campbell said it is an opportunity for several players to step up in his absence.

“We still got Mac (Alim McNeill), we’ve got Tyleik (Williams), we’ve got Levi (Onwuzurike), we’ve got (Tyler) Lacy who can play in there. It could be (Mekhi) Wingo. Could be Taki (Taimani), could be AK (Aidan Keanaaina). So we’ve got options there,” Campbell said. “But you hate to lose a player like him. He’s had a heck of a rookie season. We’ve mentioned this, but for a young guy, he’s a pro. He’s conscientious in what he did, just the right approach.”

lions.headline: NFL Week 12 power rankings: Lions a consensus Top 10 team for first time this season
lions.body:
Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell cheers on against Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the second half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Lions (8-2) are riding a six-game win streak and coming off another strong performance, beating the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 31-21 in a game that wasn’t as close as the score suggests.

The Lions land in the Top 10 in every national power ranking for the first time this season, and while most analysts are enamored with the offense—specifically superstar Jahmyr Gibbs—many still can’t get past their lack of confidence in the defense. The Lions will have a chance to change that narrative this week when they host the Chicago Bears on Thanksgiving—note: all but one ranker has the Bears ahead of the Lions, save NFL.com—but for now, they’ll remain the underdog.

Let’s take a closer look at this week’s national power rankings.

NFL.com: 5 (Previous rank: 8)

From Nick Shook:

Detroit has quietly become one of the most consistent and comfortably predictable teams in the NFL over the last two months, reliably producing offense in a fashion that is thankfully becoming less dependent on Jahmyr Gibbs, while coupling it with a defense that is steadily improving despite new injury losses. The Lions are not as flashy as the 49ers or Bears, nor are they as intimidating as Minnesota’s defense (save for Week 11), but they’re a well-rounded, winning football team that clearly isn’t going away anytime soon. Sunday’s win over the Buccaneers was just another example of this.

CBS Sports: 6 (Previous rank: 8)

From Pete Prisco:

The improvement of the defense is a good sign. They might not have Aidan Hutchinson or Jack Campbell, but they are playing much better on that side of the ball.

Sporting News: 6 (Previous rank: 8)

From Vinnie Iyer:

Jahmyr Gibbs deserves some more MVP discussion. He leads the NFL with 267 touches, 1,098 rushing yards, 1,502 scrimmage yards and 15 total TDs after scoring two more against the Buccaneers. He’s on pace for 2,550 scrimmage yards and 26 TDs, which would be one of the best running back seasons ever.

The Athletic: 6 (Previous rank: 9)

From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall:

Something to be thankful for: Ford Field

Only the Bills have won more home games since 2023 than the Lions, who improved to 5-0 at Ford Field on Sunday. They are 26-8 at home since the start of Dan Campbell’s third season. The site of Detroit’s annual Thanksgiving game, where it will be Thursday against the Bears, hasn’t always been so friendly to the home team. From 2000 to 2022, the Lions had the second-lowest home winning percentage in the league (.427).

ESPN: 6 (Previous rank: 10)

From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard:

Extension candidate: S Brian Branch

Branch and TE Sam LaPorta are playing out the 2026 season on their four-year rookie deals, but general manager Brad Holmes has reiterated that he would like to reach long-term extensions with both players, though LaPorta has expressed doubts. Branch has made an immediate impact since returning from an Achilles injury that he sustained in Week 7 of last season. In 2026, he has five passes defended and one interception in four games. Depending on how the rest of the season plays out for Branch, the Lions could use the franchise tag or agree to long-term deal with him.

USA Today: 7 (Previous rank: 10)

From Nate Davis:

RB Jahmyr Gibbs will rightly continue to command quite a bit of the spotlight as he keeps trending toward 2,500 yards from scrimmage and potentially breaking Chris Johnson’s single-season record (2,509). But how about a hand for a decimated defense that’s held up pretty well so far without injured stars Aidan Hutchinson and Jack Campbell?

Yahoo Sports: 8 (Previous rank: 11)

From Frank Schwab:

Detroit’s first defensive test without Aidan Hutchinson went well. The Lions allowed just 274 yards and 21 points, and Tampa Bay got 65 yards and a touchdown on a meaningless drive at the end of a game when Detroit led by 17 points. The Lions had four sacks, which was a good sign. The Lions’ defense has been much better since the first few weeks of the season, and Sunday’s game was without Hutchinson and linebacker Jack Campbell.

The test Thursday will be tougher, with the Chicago Bears coming in with first place in the NFC North on the line. But if Detroit’s defense can maintain this level, the Lions might be a Super Bowl contender. That could reveal itself on Thanksgiving.

“Our guys are competitive, man, and they don’t want to be counted out,” Lions head coach Dan Campbell said of the defense’s performance Sunday, via the team’s site. “And nobody cares. There are no excuses. And the only way to gain respect is just go about your business, man, and make plays and play together and prove your worth, man.”

Sports Illustrated: 10 (Previous rank: 9)

From Connor Orr:

Dan Campbell has been proven right to this point on Kelvin Sheppard. He stuck by his defensive coordinator, and now his defensive coordinator may see more head coaching interview opportunities based on how well he’s handled all of the adversity foisted onto the Lions’ defense. From Terrion Arnold to Jack Campbell to Aidan Hutchinson…it’s been a long season.

lions.headline: Film study: Jahmyr Gibbs in motion creates space for teammates
lions.body:
Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing watches a play against Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

All Grit. The Detroit Lions won their 6th straight game, knocking off the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, maintaining the top spot in the NFC North. Let’s take a look at those standings.

Breathe it in. It feels good. It feels like everything is exactly as it should be.

Ben Johnson makes his second return to Ford Field this Thanksgiving, leading the Chicago Bears into town boasting their own 8-2 record. They’re the darlings. The genius head coach. The dynamic quarterback. Every talking head’s favorite team to win the NFC.

Good.

As our own Ryan Matthews pointed out, Jared Goff looks and acts just as good as the real thing—the MVP quarterbacks who garner all of the attention—but his name isn’t Joe or Josh. That same misfit-toys metaphor applies to Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing compared to Johnson. Sure, he might be a little shorter in stature and has been given the nickname “Megamind,” but Petzing’s offense looks and plays just as well as Ben the boy wonder’s.

And if Petzing keeps getting overlooked nationally, the Lions could be fortunate enough to keep their offensive coordinator for the foreseeable future. If the stigma of his three-year stint as the playcaller in Arizona stays with him, good. Detroit will gladly retain him.

For this film study, I want to put one play design element under the microscope: presnap motion. Not just any presnap motion, but utilizing the NFL’s best offensive weapon to create space.

Stretching the seams

Todd Bowles and the Buccaneers’ defensive unit have a history of being stout, resulting in frustrating matchups for some of the NFL’s most prolific offenses. Just peek at Caleb Williams’s Week 9 box score against the Bucs: 22-for-37 with 2 touchdowns, 4 interceptions, and a cool 61.5 passer rating.

Petzing and Goff, however, diagnosed Bowles’ tendencies and stressed them. The key to it all: Jahmyr Gibbs. I don’t need to tell anyone reading this how spectacular Gibbs is with the football. But the best part of his game this weekend was how he impacted the defense without the ball.

The first two plays below are the exact same concept. Starting in shotgun with Gibbs to Goff’s right, the running back is sent in motion to the short side of the field toward an in-line tight end (Brock Wright) and Amon-Ra St. Brown outside the numbers. The cool part of the design is in the details.

Watch how Gibbs ’ wheel/fade route is run. Notably, Gibbs angles his route very wide toward the sideline hash marks, rather than pressing vertical quickly. The key here is that it forces the cover-3 cornerback to keep his drop wide, opening space for the tight end seam route.

The other key here is utilizing Jameson Williams on the field-side slot and Isaac TeSlaa outside the numbers. The passing strength of the offense, pre-motion, is to the top field-side of the screen with three eligible receivers. TeSlaa, Williams, and Gibbs. With the motion, the passing strength changes, moving the trips side to the short side. The middle single-high safety now has a choice: stay on the field-side hash to protect against Jameson Williams in the slot vertical, or lean to the now trips side with the Gibbs motion.

Good luck. Either way, he’s wrong.

On the second time below, Petzing calls the same play, but the defense tries to correct.

Notice how the cover-3 short-side corner cheats inside for the tight end vertical, but at the last second tries to shift back toward Gibbs. Goff recognizes this correction and checks down to the safety valve of St. Brown, who sides in the flat for a positive play.

Same idea, different look

Looking back at the opening series of the game, Petzing clearly had this intent of putting Gibbs in motion to stress the vertical seams in the Bucs’ zone coverage.

This time, Petzing causes the same stress using the same concept of motioning Gibbs out of the backfield, but this time from a shotgun two-back look (although the second back is actually a tight end, who runs the delayed hook route into the cleared-out zone).

But again, notice how wide Gibbs’ route is run, ultimately fading to the outside hashes. The details create the space just as much as the threat of his athleticism. Further, notice that on all three of these plays, Gibbs’ route and the tight end’s route are all run with similar depth and pacing despite having different speeds. The coverage is stressed with precision timing.

Details are the difference between good offensive coordinators and great ones. There are many coaches that can draw up a great scheme on the chalkboard Monday-Saturday. But translating speed and space from the chalkboard to the field requires precision details with a championship-level mindset.

Influencing the linebackers

Lastly, a different pre-snap motion, but with the same focus of influencing defenders to open up space. This time, the goal is to influence the linebackers and create space in the zone for Amon-Ra St. Brown. Notice how quickly Alex Anzalone reacts to the motion to get horizontal from the field-side linebacker position. St. Brown is able to swiftly find and sit in the opening created for an easy pitch-and-catch.

It’s a short week with the Bears coming in on Thursday for the big Thanksgiving showdown. But even with less practice time to prepare, I expect Petzing will have his wrinkle of the week, targeting what Dan, Drew, Jared, and the rest of the offensive staff diagnose as the weakness and tendency of the Bears’ defense.

Embrace the fight. Appreciate the opportunity. Keep the edge.

It feels too soon to lose Etta, a developmental guy who was still an overgrown edge last year and will be used for four-year build-a-bear projects in the forever hereafter. He's been Michigan's #1 DT for most of the season now, which is not something I had on my bingo card.
Things he does well now are the kinds of things you have to develop in an S&C program and constant reps with the sleds. Michigan's stunts with other DTs have been largely ineffective this year. Etta here demonstrates why it's important for the tackle to be doing the heavy lifting—literally—on those.

The explosion to get upfield quickly is the first ingredient. That's what frightens the RG and creates extra space in the A gap between the G and the C (#54) just above Etta.

Etta's quickness and power get him into the RT before that guy has a chance to notice Nichols coming around and call out. Look at the space this has created for Nichols to rush up the middle.

Etta's speed was always a positive for him when chasing QBs into the flat, but it's that speed and awareness that have been generating stuffs near the line of scrimmage that are not usually plays a guy in his position is expected to be part of. This zone run to the left is supposed to get #58 across Etta, who's lined up like a 3-4 DE and will be the backside edge of a play meant to go far frontside.

Etta doesn't just stay playside; he stays clean enough to run across the surface of the run and get to the ballcarrier. We don't notice these things live, but they come out a lot in the charting. After an offseason when Etta was assumed to be going to Texas A&M until Michigan came back with whatever Texas A&M was offering, I think Etta's season warrants whatever that was. Yes, even if it was more than Pierce's cut, although Pierce (the next DT over, getting held in the play above) was every bit as critical to this year's defense being consistently good up front even after the season's goals were out of reach.
Speaking of Pierce, he came in with a typical high score, but this one was a little different in that it was made with BIG LOUD plays, not lots of pretty good ones.

[link]
He was my runner up for which Hassan Haskins Memorial jersey to get last offseason. I wound up with Jalen Hoffman, which worked out, but Pierce was the correct answer. He was the dude still going hard in the late drives against Ohio State, and the guy doing that again vs MSU this year.
The thing with Pierce this season however is he would sometimes disappear for long stretches. This was in part because offenses didn't bother trying to run his way, but this didn't stop Etta and Lea'ea from generating bigger numbers. It hit me with this game when I noticed he kept trotting off the field in 3rd & short and 3rd & long situations. Why would you want (one of) your best tackle(s) on the bench for those moments? I have a two-part hypothesis:
Part 1 is Pierce can't help himself. Every time he's on the field he goes all out. I've lost track of the games where he starts with +0.5 events that are irrelevant to the play but too good not to chart on early drives. Then he's worn out and we spend the rest of the game chasing dominant Pierce.
A more judicial use of Pierce netted a stronger result: more +2 events, and this +3.

[link]
Those are often more valuable on standard downs, when you can get the offense off-schedule, than key downs, when they're expecting the DT at the most likely point of attack to be coming in hard and low off the snap.
Part 2 is I think this comes down to Jay Hill's philosophy with DTs. The Ravens way was to have big pluggers soaking up space and attention so there was no room to run inside. It was effective, but also expensive, and we needed about five DTs ready to sub in for any game. Hill goes for more of a Don Brown approach, asking his DTs to shoot upfield and cause havoc. If you get it right, you can get TFLs of 2 or more yards, which changes the game state more than consistently holding an offense to 0-1 yards.

[link]
You see Lea'ea's explosion and the importance of getting to the ball before the RB can start getting downfield of Boney's contact with the trap blocker that Lea'ea was following. You also see Etta, at nose, where a double-team doesn't really do much to the plan. If you're going to play this way, you don't need Trey Pierce blasting the C backwards. It's valuable, sure, but you can use him in other spots.
Plus, Lea'ea is just killing it these days. I started the season down on him because his Utah film showed him getting blown out three plays in four. Now that's maybe once or twice a game, and the return is tenfold in the disruption he's causing to OL trying to get a double going.
#91 at nose

[link]
If he does this against Ohio State we have three star DTs.
Do we have star edges back?
I would say John Henry Daley and Dominic Nichols are, respectively, Back and Mostly Back from injuries earlier in the year.
JHD left edge, Nichols right:

[link]
We need to be careful because the UCLA OTs are probably not that good; the LT got a cyan from Alex and the RT is an injury replacement. But that weird bend that belies JHD's size and playing style has been missing all year, and I worried it was a permanent casualty of his Achilles injury. I thought I saw it again in the above. It's just ghostly...he's pass rushing and then two frames later he's turned ninety degrees. This drew several links in his recruiting profile, but I think the above is the first instance at Michigan.
Nichols also missed time with injury this year, and was notably hobbling on one foot when he was on the field. His burst returns weekly, and whether it was the UCLA right tackle or the onset of health, he took another step forward in getting back the rush that terrorized the nonconference schedule. He also was the guy I tagged for missing a stunt call.
#8 DE on the top:

[link]
Fortunately the WR dropped it and no damage was incurred from the rustiness.
One reason I had to wonder if it was Nichols making the RT his personal turnstile or if this was a public service that guy (Jaylan Jeffers, an Oregon transfer) offers to everybody was Tariq Boney was also back to his nonconference form, IE a Tasmanian Devil.

[link]
I'm so worried about Boney bias now that I timed the impact to around the RT to confirm Tariq is making that turn as quickly as I think he is. It's about 0.65 seconds. Jeffers is a 7th year senior who was once a 2020 Oregon commit comped to former UCLA OT Caleb Benenoch—a long-armed OT who should have been able to deploy the grabby technique that's been slowing Boney's pass rush the last few weeks. My inexpert analysis is the grab-and-rip move above was a lot more economical than I saw from Boney earlier in the season. He's progressing, and it's causing extreme havoc like Dieffenbach letting go of the ball before throwing it.

[link]
I didn't have that many events from Benny Patterson; the one that stood out is he lost an edge. The notable thing about his events are they're more mistakes than physical issues, which is what you'd expect from young players.
What about the mistakes from old players? You know: the ones that caused overtime?
The fanbase at large is down on Smith Snowden, enough that I'm taking heat for being positive about him in the preseason. He had some big busts against Oregon, and he had one of the more consequential missed solo tackles of the season.

[link]
Fine, I gave him a –2 for that. He's not a good tackler. I'm sure that's why the coaches initially put Snowden outside and Berry at nickel, despite the universe and Berry himself (I'm sure) arguing he's really a cornerback. Brian and I had it out whether I said Snowden was Sainristil; my scouting report called him Zeke Berry, and I used the hot takes segment of our preview podcast to make the comp to Sainristil coming from the program, but in terms that were clear I didn't believe it. I was much higher on him than what we've seen down the stretch; Zeke Berry is a compliment.
But the reason it feels SO bad is the game state when Snowden makes mostly square contact with Wayne Knight three yards behind the line of scrimmage with a full head of steam.

Mike Sainristil drives through that tackle and makes it 4th & 12 with no timeouts. Zeke Berry...would miss that tackle sometimes. Knight has a 22% missed tackle rate this year according to PFF; this was actually a worse game than usual for him. And we need to give Snowden some credit for staying in position to take away Semaj Morgan until the second he read the pass, then zipping to meet its recipient three yards in the backfield. In our minds the tackle is the easy part, and that overshadows the fact he gets the hard part done more often than not.
It also feels bad because Snowden was the guy who got out-physicaled in a mana-a-mano play versus Semaj on the 4th down earlier in the drive.

[link]
Showing up for big moments is the way you become a program legend, and to a degree I do believe there's a kind of guy who meets those moments well. Snowden just isn't that guy. He has more good plays than bad plays, and they're randomly interspersed through the football game.

[link]
The thing about Snowden and Berry is I really did nail that comp, and that's a problem because both of these players are best put at cornerback, and both are built more like nickels, which is sometimes a problem at cornerback. This is the play after the the missed tackle on 3rd & 9.
#10 CB on the bottom

[link]
Berry can't afford to slow up even a little bit. He is fast but not THAT fast. He doesn't have great size. The throw here is into a small window ("the hole" in Cover 2) that NFL passing games will attack mercilessly if Berry or Snowden get to spend any time there, but if you lose one play like this per game in the NFL that's better than replacement NFL cornerbacking.
The problem, if we're being honest, isn't with either of these guys. The problem is Michigan doesn't have a real nickel, so they're forced to use the two most nickel-shaped objects in the role. If Shamari Earls or Jo'Ziah Stewart had taken a step forward you could have moved Jyaire Hill into the slot, but you can't move Hill now when the greatest college receiver of all time is next on the docket. You can't trade Smith or Berry. And you can't rotate them to keep them fresh because their next cornerback is, for some reason, Jeremiah Earby, who looks more like the Caleb Anderson end of aged grad transfer corners thus far.
Also remember the thing I said about tackling being a thing that comes with tired players? Does it mean something that Snowden's was play #9 of the drive? Earby was on the field for the last third of this drive, which made me upset because there were a few moments Michigan really could have used Hill's tackling (the run to get them to 1st & Goal especially). But look at the snap counts for the corners: 64 for Jyaire, 62 or Snowden, 69 for Berry. These guys don't get many breaks, and are chasing these receivers around the field in man coverage. The problem isn't that Snowden sucks; it's that the cornerback rotation should be these three guys with one or two nickels.
Last week I wrote Snowden must feel a certain way about missing hometown Utah's championship run; I got some feedback from a Michigan insider that Smith was asked about this off the record, and offendedly said he'd transfer to Michigan again. Is that bravado? Sure, but it's the kind of bullshit I like from my football players (you can be honest about this stuff later, like Rod Moore). I tell you this because I do think it's caused a bit of bias in me that I had to keep in mind while charting him, and there are people (not Brian) accusing me of being soft on Smith to be precious about a preseason take I didn't have. That sort of accusation gets under my skin because I believe the thing that actually makes me worthy of writing this piece is I'm good at (working my ass off and) identifying my biases before they get into the numbers. If you're going to say I'm the kind of guy who might buy a Snowden jersey that's true, but you should know it's mostly because I hear he's a Good Dude.
Snowden could return to Michigan for a fifth year and I hope he does, because we need OUTSIDE cornerbacks next year. Jyaire certainly isn't sticking around—UCLA knew not to test him in coverage so Hill's strong score was from his work as a run defender—and both Berry and Earby are out of eligibility. They need to find a nickel.
Question...and sorry if this has been answered before. Who TF is Jeremiah Earby?
A Boise State (previously Cal) five-year transfer who was in Roddy Gayle purgatory until a few weeks ago.
And he's playing ahead of five-star Shamari Earls because...?
I assume Earls is in the portal at this point; he was responsible for some of the big busts early in the season. It's a bummer; in a program that was more locked in I imagine we'd see Earls peeking through by now.
Speaking of players I don't recognize, who was Linebacker #30 who started? Another Roddy situation?
That was Max Alford. A BYU depth guy who followed Jay Hill and has another year to play. His YMRMFSPA last summer was Devin Gil. I was not enthused.
Projection: Deep backup/student-athlete who might contribute on special teams and be a good locker room dude to help integrate the new players and staff then go into coaching.

Why was Max Alford starting?
I assume this was an accountability thing from Taylor and Bowles last week. Nathaniel Staehling also started, though he's now firmly—snaps-wise—the 3rd linebacker on this team. Owusu-Boateng has been LB4 but he didn't play well at Oregon either. So they gave Alford a shot.
And did it work out for us?
Not really. When I went through the LB transfer class I was impressed by Staehling's headiness and thought Moa was miscast as a "linebacker" when he was really an old fashioned 4-3 Under SAM (i.e. a DE/LB hybrid). Everybody else I figured was depth. Alford doesn't have much athletic upside, doesn't have much size, and despite spending more time in Jay Hill's system than anybody else on this team, he doesn't really know where to go.
#30 middle linebacker

[link]
The big hit from Rod Moore needed a heroic save from the safety because the linebacker supposed to tackle that after a few years stepped out of the way.
#LB 30 on the top hash.

[link]
I do think Alford might have some value as a coverage linebacker if Taylor is unavailable; Alford doesn't cover grass.
Alford's playing time is more of a statement on Chase Taylor. I didn't want to dive too deep into last week's disastrous play because it felt like dogpiling on a guy when he's down, and the talent there is so evident I'm still very excited about Taylor's future. He should have been afforded the opportunity to play 2023 Jimmy Rolder behind Cole Sullivan's Michael Barrett (Sullivan has been wasted at Oklahoma FWIW) instead of having to sink or swim as a sophomore.
The Chase Taylor issues are still 100% mental, but they're still –2 mental breakdowns. Taylor was the guy who left his receiver unattended on the 2nd & 8 that got UCLA into field goal range with 14 seconds left in the 2nd quarter. Taylor was the guy who let the tight end leak out uncovered on the "Nice Throw" that led off the game column. Taylor was the guy who left the tight end open that Madden Iamaleava decided to ignore. Taylor also picked up a bunch of –1s in run defense while learning how to play a zone read off a blitz, or like when he got caught trying to time the snap count.
Much of the "they're very good down to down but sometimes they give up a 3rd & long in the middle" nature of this defense often comes down to Chase Taylor being a developmental second year player forced into starting too early. This isn't all about his coverage, but how Jay tries to mitigate it by having Taylor pass rush more often than he should for Taylor's (currently) limited pass rush arsenal. He rarely, if ever, wins a one-on-one rush despite starting with good leverage against a bad tackle, because he understandably hasn't the block destruction that even dedicated pass-rushers need years to develop.
I'm starting to believe the "Winkish" over-use of those cute pressures I complained about earlier in the season is just a reaction to Taylor's current coverage limitations. Michigan often blitzes on 3rd (and 4th) downs, or runs Amoeba coverages that put, e.g., Benny Patterson in a curl/flat zone while Taylor is edge rushing from the other side. Offenses are ready for them, preparing quick throws for key downs, and triangle reads that target zones likely to be covered be DL. That means you're not running enough base in those situations. This hit me when they brought a WLB fire blitz near the end of the 2nd quarter and UCLA used a quick rub route to get five yards and out of bounds, turning a difficult FGA into an average one. Is this really Jay Hill trying to be the hero with a playcall, or is he looking at his personnel and thinking he's better off giving Chris Bracy or Jyaire Hill a shot at making a PLAY than risking Taylor blowing a coverage for big yards?
One use they did find for Taylor in this game was as a spy who can leap into throwing lanes. Dude has basketball ups, and knocked down an RPO that looked like it had legs by hiding out behind the line. He came close to doing it again on the 4th & 6 near the end of regulation.

The arc Dieffenbach had to add to that pass could have been relevant if Snowden wasn't knocked back so far on contact with the receiver. I still really like Chase Taylor, and think he's a priority to bring back next year.
What about a fifth year from Bowles?
Man I would love that. The Oregon game was the part of Billy Madison when everything he was working for had failed and Billy went back to being a shiftless lay about—I think. I actually haven't watched this stupid movie since college. I know there's a jeopardy game at the end because there's that one quotable line from James Downey in it that I'm saving for a –2 moment against Ohio State.
Billy Madisonly speaking, that puts the UCLA performance in that space between the 2nd and 3rd acts when Billy has been convinced to give up chasing imaginary penguins for good, but needs to study up for the big exam. This is where we see how much he's learned, as the kind of trick question that previously messed him up entirely receives a straightforward, confident answer.
MLB #18 (blue arrow)

[link]
That was a cute design—the read is a fake to set up the RB as a lead blocker—meant to get the MLB to the RB's side to take a false step with the blocking and bump into his mate trying to read the quarterback. Bowles stays on assignment, follows the RB to the ball, and makes the play, also critically staying out of Staehling's path as the heady WLB diagnoses the play's direction and slips past the TE meant to downblock him.
Staehling is out of eligibility, but I feel like Michigan can find another guy like him (and should, every year) in the FCS or mid-major ranks.
Anything from various Michigan head coaching candidates?
UCLA had a lot of cute stuff prepared for this game. I don't think it was to make a showing in the Big House or because Bob Chesney was subtly slipping us his resume. Teams (not Michigan this year; they're still trying out different bases) often get to this part of the season with a bunch of wrinkles off their base they've practiced but haven't been able to use, and they come out the week before Rivalry Week to get the rival thinking about them. There's that trick above, which they ran twice and will get USC thinking twice about having the backside LB overplay inside zone during a zone read mesh. There's also this thing I called "Midline Veer" with a TE fold that they didn't get blocked up correctly (the puller needs to get Moa):

[link]
If you're evaluating Chesney, there was a bit of a "trying to hard" to their offense that ultimately hurt them in this game because of execution errors on their part and Michigan's (fan-motivated!!!?) focused play part. In the other UCLA games I watched this worked out for them, so it's not a negative, just a gentle reminder to keep things simple three timezones away before the greatest fans in American sports.
I was going to have a section here about Jay Hill overblitzing, but I moved that to the Taylor talk once I realized the likely rationale behind it. This also makes me a little more confident in Jay Hill. If Raver thinks she needs too much time to get her athletic director hire right to get on the head coaching carousel (deadline: Christmas week), I could support giving Jay the interim tag for a year. Whittingham still needs to go.
Anything to get off your chest?
I've come full circle on Whittingham's refusal to support his players with the officials. Like his "Hate is a strong word" response to the Ohio State rivalry, what I had hoped was a sign of a deeper understanding was really more evidence this guy has completely checked out.

What I took for a strategic attempt to curry favor with the pedantic weenies until there's something major to complain about was really apathy all along. Watch what happens to Taylor on the backside of this end-around:
#4 lined up at the bottom

[link]
This wasn't a "Refs*" game any more than normal, so this isn't a shot at them. They miss things sometimes. But when they miss something that egregious you have to point it out to them so it's in their minds, right? This gain led to points before the half, and UCLA's drive after the half featured several really bad missed calls. My theory on buzzing the officials is you wait until it's something they clearly would have called if they saw it, and then they feel bad and pay better attention. When you're not in their minds at all, they miss even the pedantic things that all officials secretly love to call, like a screen that steps well over the line of scrimmage:

[link]
No conspiracy. Just humans who act as humans are wont, and the only football coach in America not obsessively using that to his advantage.
* [Notice I'm trying really hard to say "officials" not "refs" because the referee is only one official.]

Heroes? Bracy, Pierce, Etta, Jyaire, Moore, Daley, and Ice Moa—all seniors I might add—plus Boney, and Michigan fans everywhere who came and cheered their team, or gave up their tickets to those who would.

Maybe not so heroic? Snowden picks bad times for his bad plays. Chase Taylor has the Moutonishness of the young. Zeke Berry let some of the Old Zeek creep back in. Benny Patterson is another young showing his age. UCLA's receivers had a bad game (five drops), but then we covered that in the heroes.

What does it mean for The Game and beyond?
It would be nice to retain the DTs. I assume Jyaire and Bracy are NFL-bound—no regrets—but Lea'ea and Etta are still a bit small for the NFL, and Pierce could raise his stock considerably with a little more stamina and a staff that better gets his nuances. Three good DTs are an extremely valuable commodity these days.
I know how the Troy Bowles story goes. Stupid happy ending, then a bowl game where they ship the imaginary penguin. You don't have to get this reference; in fact you are probably better off if you don't. Just saying Bowles has come a really long way and if we don't get him back I'm going to remember him fondly.
Taylor, Boney, and Patterson are the youts to be excited for. This a weird year when the defense is mostly made of 4th year guys with 1st and 2nd year guys buried, but there are at least three pieces who look like long term Wolverines whose careers are going to be really good when they're ready. None are quite there, which influences how they're used.
I can endorse Jay Hill as Interim HC for 2027. I finally made sense of his tendency to Wink out on critical downs—he's trying to put it on his senior playmakers not the youts—and while he needs to adjust to the fact he's been adjusted to, I get it. We just talked about how Lloyd Carr was the rarest thing in football: an excellent coach who a) isn't insane or b) therefore trying to get out of college and to the pros as quickly as possible. Jay Hill is giving off those vibes.
Pretty cool moment as a fired up #Michigan DC Jay Hill celebrates in the tunnel with several players like LB Troy Bowles and DE Dominic Nichols following the overtime win over No. 4 UCLA. https://t.co/1rLsIDxOWM
— Brice Marich (@BriceMarich) November 22, 2026

Beat Ohio If vibes matter, I'm interested to see how The Ohio State fans react to their first three-loss team in a The Game at The Shoe since 2004, and the first four-loss team since...uh...the 1960s? [checks]. 1988. The Ohio State fans have been pretty hard on their lads in the best of times. Michigan Stadium's vibes were rancid before halftime against MSU and I think that contributed to the team's performance in that one too.

michigan.headline: Ryan Day is hopeful Ohio State can overcome its ‘frustration’ with a win over Michigan
michigan.body:
LINCOLN, NEBRASKA - NOVEMBER 21: Head coach Ryan Day of the Ohio State Buckeyes stands with the team before the game against the Nebraska Cornhuskers at Memorial Stadium on November 21, 2026 in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Steven Branscombe/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Heading into the week of The Game, this year’s matchup between Michigan and Ohio State has already taken on a much different tone. Not so long ago, both teams would enter the final week of the regular season walking the ultimate tightrope in the hopes of clinching a trip to the Big Ten title game or College Football Playoff, but this year, neither team is playing for either.

Of course, we didn’t always think it’d end up this way. Back in August, Ohio State was ranked as the No. 1 team in the AP’s preseason poll, and many thought that Michigan could enter this matchup in the range of 8-3 or 9-2 with a shot to bolster its playoff resume. Not so much, though, as the Buckeyes are clinging to the No. 25 spot in the AP poll, and Michigan only clinched bowl eligibility last week with an upset win over UCLA.

As the kids say, both teams are down bad, but the momentum likely sits on Michigan’s side thanks to its win last week and Ohio State’s loss on the road to Nebraska.

Following the loss, an emotional Carson Hinzman captured much of the feeling of Ohio State’s team right now with how the season has gone for the Buckeyes, lamenting how “heartbreaking” it was for his team to come up short against Nebraska.

"This sucks. You give everything to a program and come up short it's heartbreaking"

A really emotional moment during the presser from Carson Hinzman: pic.twitter.com/IMtdmFJTeI
— Adam King (@AdamKing10TV) November 21, 2026

Now with one game left, Ohio State head coach Ryan Day will be tasked with getting his team psyched back up again to take the field against their bitter rivals.

“For the guys in this room at this point, nothing else matters, because there’s nothing we can do about what’s gone on in the past,” Day told reporters on Tuesday. “We need to win this game. That’s just how it goes, because we need to win this game every year. When we put our list of all the things that are important, that’s the No. 1 goal. Not the only goal. . . But this one, right here, is at No. 1 at the top.”

On the heels of a bad loss, Ohio State will have to do plenty from an emotional and schematic standpoint to get itself back on track. Michigan is far from the best opponent Ohio State will have seen, but it doesn’t mean the game will be a cakewalk either, mostly due to Jay Hill’s dominant defense that’s kept Michigan in nearly every game this year. Day acknowledged that the frustration has been real this season, and he believes the onus is on him to get everyone re-focused ahead of the biggest game of the year.

“Frustration is real, and I’m as frustrated as anybody, but it’s ultimately my job, so I have to get it right. It doesn’t do me any good to be frustrated. That being said, I think we all want to respond better and want to see the response better,” Day said.

The result in The Game can change perceptions for both sides, with the 2024 matchup being a perfect example. Michigan’s upset win over the Buckeyes is looked back on fondly despite the Wolverines finishing the season at 7-5. At the same time, Ohio State wound up winning the National Championship two months later, but with an ugly loss still on its resume. 2026 has been a season to forget for both sides, but either can rinse the taste out of its mouth a bit with a win on Saturday.

“The Game is still the game. We’re playing on Saturday, and it means everything to us,” Day added.

When the teams take the field on Saturday, it’ll be the first time since 1966 that both will enter the game with at least four losses already. It’s hard to fathom that a Michigan win would mean that both teams finish the season at 7-5 – a long way off from the preseason expectations from both sides.

The hatred is still very real, though, even if the matchup lacks the stakes it had even just three or four years ago; this week, it merely represents a good chance for both sides to take their anger and “frustrations” out on each other.

michigan.headline: Warde Manuel to stay on job until Michigan finds new AD, per report
michigan.body:
Michigan athletic director Warde Manuel looks on during warmups before the game between Ohio State and Michigan at Ohio Stadium in Columbus, Ohio on Saturday, Nov. 30, 2024. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

It’s been a good week for Michigan athletic director Warde Manuel. First, he somehow received a game ball from Kyle Whittingham after Michigan’s win over UCLA, and now he’ll be staying on the job a while longer after Michigan botched and rescinded the hiring of Trev Alberts.

Per a report from ESPN, Manuel met with incoming Michigan president C. Cybele Raver and Manuel “agreed to stay in the job until the school finds a new athletic director.”

Michigan AD Warde Manuel has agreed to stay in the job until the school finds a new athletic director. He informed the staff this after meeting with new president C. Cybele Raver, sources tell me and @DanWetzel.
— Pete Thamel (@PeteThamel) November 25, 2026

Alberts was supposed to officially start at Michigan on Dec. 1, but it appears the athletic director search could linger well past that. There was speculation Michigan could go the interim athletic director route — it certainly worked when Jim Hackett hired Jim Harbaugh — instead, Raver opts to keep a man in charge in Warde Manuel, who’s had far more controversies than Trev Alberts.

How this will impact whether Kyle Whittingham remains Michigan’s head football coach is unknown. Would Manuel have the power to fire Whittingham despite being a lame duck? Would he even want to fire someone he hired last year?

This is a mess. A self-inflicted mess from new ‘leadership’ at the university.

michigan.headline: Hello Warde Manuel

msu.headline: We Have Come to the End
msu.body:
A wide shot of the exterior of SHI Stadium, the home field of the Rutgers Scarlet Knights, before an NCAA FBS football game in Piscataway, United States, on October 3, 2026. (Photo by Dan Squicciarini/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images

Well, TOC, here we are.  At the end of another difficult football season, in this situation:

Michigan State has to beat Rutgers, on the road (Saturday, 4:15 PM ET, Big Ten Network), to earn a tie for last place in the 18-team Big Ten Conference.  They will be tasked with doing so, perhaps without their first and second string quarterbacks, and numerous other key players on both sides of the ball.

This article gets published before the first required football availability report, which comes out later tonight, but MSU QB Alessio Milivojevic took a hard hit to his left side / left arm two games ago against Washington.  He was seen on the sideline Friday against Oregon wearing a substantial brace.  I have no idea what specific type of injury this would be supporting, but it just seems unlikely that it would heal up in time for Saturday.

On top of all this, the Spartans are coming off a 45-7 beatdown at the hands of Oregon while Rutgers is riding high after a 25-24 win over Penn State, their first in Happy Valley since 1988.

Ok, this is enough negativity for one article.  Let’s look for some positives.

While the Spartans’ record and standing in the Big Ten has not improved this year, things still feel different.  MSU has responded to bad losses early in the season to Nebraska and Wisconsin.  They’ve continued to play hard and came up just short to Illinois, Northwestern, and Washington.  Regardless of what happens on Saturday in New Jersey, the season will be most remembered for the win at Michigan, which showed the culture and style of play Pat Fitzgerald is trying to recreate at MSU.

However, it would still be nice to build off the UM win with something other than a close loss to Washington.  That will hopefully come via a solid transfer portal haul in January but a win at Rutgers certainly wouldn’t hurt MSU as they plan their portal possibilities.

In 2024, under Jonathan Smith, Michigan State had a nice 32-20 win against Iowa in mid-October and then a real chance to win at Michigan the following Saturday.  The Spartans blew that chance in Ann Arbor and then got blown out by Indiana and Illinois.  The season ended with a 41-14 home loss to Rutgers that kept the Spartans from bowl eligibility and was every bit as bad as the score would indicate.

Many might argue that the final nail in Smith’s coffin at MSU was the 2025 Homecoming loss to UCLA but perhaps it all started by failing to capitalize on that Iowa win two years ago.

I don’t know if the Spartans will win at Rutgers on Saturday but I also don’t see this season ending like it did in 2024.  Michigan State will, once again, come to play.  A victory might hinge on if third string quarterback Kayd Coffman can stay consistent, manage a whole game, and avoid turnovers.  We’ll look at keys to the game at the end but first, let’s take a closer look at how Rutgers compares to MSU.
